title: Exploring the relationship between health literacy and attitude to believe fake news about food: a survey among the Italian population
screen_reason: Cross-sectional self-administered online survey of 2,284 community-pharmacy customers across Italy (January-March 2024). Although the paper's aim is the health-literacy correlation, it reports descriptive shares of respondents who encountered food-related fake news at a stated frequency (21.5% at least once a week) and who admitted sharing it online (37.4%), both with a stated denominator -> RECALL (exposure and sharing). Belief figures (78% believed such news; 42.8% endorsing the gluten-free myth) are excluded by the instructions.

estimates.country: Italy (nine community pharmacies in northern, central and southern Italy)
estimates.platform: Survey (self-reported encounters with food-related fake news 'on the Web'; no single platform named)
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who report encountering food-related fake news at least once a week
estimates.denominator: 2,284 pharmacy customers aged 18-75 recruited by QR code at nine community pharmacies in northern, central and southern Italy (convenience sample; pharmacies chosen purposively for geographic balance: 49.9% north/centre, 50.1% south/islands)
estimates.definition: Selected the 'at least once a week' frequency band on the ad hoc item asking how often the respondent comes across food-related fake news; the questionnaire illustrated the concept with concrete examples of popular web food fake news (e.g. 'gluten-free diet without coeliac disease'). Falsity is the respondent's own judgement.
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition is given for the survey item; the paper's framing is "disinformation, content intentionally crafted to mislead or deceive" and "'nutrition fake', a widespread proliferation of fake nutrition information online". The authors explicitly note that "no internationally standardised definition of food-related fake news currently exists".
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Fake news and related variables', p. 5
estimates.ground_truth_detail: No external verification: the respondent decides what counts as food-related fake news, prompted by illustrative examples in the questionnaire. The four fake-news items were ad hoc, pretested for clarity on a pilot of 300 people but, as the authors state, "not formally validated".

estimates.country: Italy (nine community pharmacies in northern, central and southern Italy)
estimates.platform: Survey (self-reported sharing on the respondent's own social profiles / social networks)
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who admit to having shared food-related fake news on their own social profiles
estimates.denominator: 2,284 pharmacy customers aged 18-75 recruited at nine community pharmacies in northern, central and southern Italy
estimates.definition: Gave any answer other than 'never' on the ad hoc 5-point item ('every day'/'always' to 'never') asking about the respondent's own experience of sharing fake food news on their social profiles
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition; the paper's framing is "disinformation, content intentionally crafted to mislead or deceive" and "'nutrition fake', a widespread proliferation of fake nutrition information online".
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Fake news and related variables', p. 5
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Self-reported behaviour with respondent-defined falsity; the authors flag social-desirability and recall bias as a limitation, mitigated only by anonymity. Items were pretested but not formally validated.
estimates.moderator_quote: assessed by four ad hoc items on a 5-­point category
estimates.notes: This is observed-behaviour SELF-REPORT, not a hypothetical sharing intention, so it is inside scope as RECALL/sharing rather than being excluded as an intention measure. The exact threshold that produced 37.4% ('admitted to sharing it') is not spelled out; from the item design it must be everything above 'never'. Self-reported sharing of misinformation is systematically under-reported, so treat 37.4% as a lower bound. Confidence medium: unvalidated item, convenience sample, social-desirability pressure. | QUOTE NOTE: two-column PDF, sentence split across text lines. missed_or_uncertain: (1) 'several times a month (52.7%)' is a separate frequency band of the same exposure item; it is stated verbatim but is not cumulative, and combining it with the 21.5% band to get an 'at least monthly' figure would be a cross-category sum barred by R8. An adjudicator who wants a broader exposure band should note that no such cumulative figure appears anywhere in the paper. (2) All belief figures are excluded by the instructions: 'About 78% stated they "often" or "sometimes" believed such news'; '42.8% of respondents believe that, even without a gluten allergy or intolerance, it is healthier to follow a gluten-free diet; only 36.7% disagree, while 20.5% remain uncertain'; and the cross-tabulation figures 21.8% (of never-sharers) and 77.8% (of self-reported sharers) endorsing the gluten-free myth, which are belief shares within sharing subgroups. (3) '48.8% ... bought food or supplements due to social media advertising' and '49.6% admitted to following dietary advice from influencers or celebrities' are advertising/influencer susceptibility, not misinformation exposure. (4) The HLS-EU-Q6 item frequencies (e.g. 61.6% reporting difficulty assessing the reliability of health information from media sources) measure health literacy, not misinformation prevalence. (5) The logistic regression ORs are effect estimates, not shares, and in any case are internally inconsistent - see rob.

rob.design: Cross-sectional self-administered online survey (Google Forms). Sampling frame: convenience sample of 2,284 customers aged 18-75 at nine community pharmacies in northern, central and southern Italy, the pharmacies chosen by purposive non-probabilistic sampling for geographic balance; participants recruited January-March 2024 by a QR code at the entrance or handed out by pharmacists, with pharmacists giving in-person help to those with limited digital literacy. Participation voluntary and anonymous with explicit informed consent; ethics approval University of Foggia protocol 162/CE/2024. No response rate is reported (the number invited is unknown), so the denominator is those who chose to respond. Instrument: 27 items in five sections, piloted on 300 people not in the final analysis; health literacy measured with the validated Italian HLS-EU-Q6 (Cronbach alpha 0.81, McDonald omega 0.81), but the four fake-news items were ad hoc and, in the authors' words, 'not formally validated'. Data cleaning: questionnaires with >25% missing responses, logically inconsistent entries and duplicates removed; missing data <5% per variable, listwise deletion in regressions. Analysis: Welch's ANOVA with Bonferroni correction and eta-squared, chi-square tests, binary logistic regression (VIF <2, Box-Tidwell), SPSS v29. NO CODING PROCEDURE OR INTER-RATER RELIABILITY APPLIES - falsity is entirely self-defined. Authors' limitations: non-probabilistic pharmacy sampling limits generalisability, rural populations may be under-represented, self-report brings recall and social-desirability bias, cross-sectional design precludes causal inference, and no standardised definition of food-related fake news exists. ADDITIONAL RELIABILITY CONCERNS FOUND IN THE TEXT (not acknowledged by the authors): Table 2 lists the education contrasts against a middle-school reference ('High school diploma vs middle school diploma' OR 2.45; 'Degree vs middle school diploma' OR 2.46) while the narrative reports the same two ORs as middle-school and high-school respondents having higher odds than university graduates - the reference category is stated inconsistently and the direction of the education effect therefore cannot be resolved from the paper; 'Unemployed vs government employee' and 'Student vs government employee' carry an identical OR of 7.01 with identical confidence limits (4.600-10.865), which is a duplicated table row; and the narrative attributes OR 2.04 to 'workers' whereas Table 2 gives Worker OR 1.09, p=0.766 (non-significant) and Self-employed OR 2.07. Table 1's geographic counts sum to 2,283 rather than 2,284.
rob.item6_quote: Attitude in believing and sharing fake news online: respondents' self-reported experience of believing and sharing fake food news on their social profiles was assessed by four ad hoc items on a 5-point category scale from 'every day' (or 'always') to 'never'.
rob.item10_quote: A substantial portion of respondents reported encountering food-related fake news at least once a week (21.5%) or several times a month (52.7%). About 78% stated they 'often' or 'sometimes' believed such news, and 37.4% admitted to sharing it.
